questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
Given that $\lambda =-3$ and $\lambda =4$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-10 & -7 \\ 14 & 11\end{aligned}]$,
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & -7 \\ 14 & 11\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -7 \\ 14 & 14\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-7{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2}=0 \\ 14{x}_{1}+14{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -7 & 0 \\ 14 & 14 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-7 & -7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For $\lambda =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & -7 \\ 14 & 11\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-14 & -7 \\ 14 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-14{x}_{1}-7{x}_{2}=0 \\ 14{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-14 & -7 & 0 \\ 14 & 7 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-14 & -7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to an Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
Find an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}16 & -30 \\ 9 & -17\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}16 & -30 \\ 9 & -17\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -30 \\ 9 & -15\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}18{x}_{1}-30{x}_{2}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}-15{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -30 & 0 \\ 9 & -15 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}18 & -30 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
18{x}_{1}-30{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -6 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 & 0 \\ 3 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
Given that $\lambda =3$ and $\lambda =10$ are the eigenvalues of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}]$,
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately. 

- For $\lambda =3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain  ${x}_{1}=-3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For $\lambda =10,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 
From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, two linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix $A$ are

$$
[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{2}{9}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
